title.text:
Binary classification (yes or
no) and how to measure it

objects.text: Can a binary classifier say yes or no to "high energy demand", how does it learn, and how do we count and price its mistakes?

CML3113  |  Mining and Petroleum Engineering  |  Week 9, class 2 of 4  |  Friday 13 November 2026, 08:00 to 11:00
KLAi  |  International University of East Africa  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome to Class 2. Last week the model gave you a number. Today it answers yes or no, which is called binary classification. We stay with the crusher data, and the question is whether the crusher energy demand reaches its limit. You will see how a classifier is built, how it learns from its errors, and the most important lesson of the day: how to count its mistakes and put a price on them. The ideas come first, then the lab, then the quiz.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Turn the crusher energy demand into a binary label with a limit, and standardise the features with the mean and standard deviation
Train logistic regression and a decision tree classifier, and explain how logistic regression learns: log loss and gradient descent
Count TP, FN, FP and TN, work out precision, recall and F1, and choose a decision threshold with a cost table

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can turn the crusher energy demand into a binary label using a limit, and standardise the features using the mean and the standard deviation. You can train two classifiers and explain how logistic regression learns, with log loss and gradient descent.

And you can count the four kinds of answer, work out precision, recall and F1, and choose a decision threshold from a cost table. In the last 20 minutes the Block 1 quiz opens online, and part B of the Block 1 assignment repeats today's lab.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is a baseline model for?
2.  What does the unit of the MAE tell you?
3.  Why do we split the rows by equipment group?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Class 1. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is a baseline model for? Take a moment.

A good answer: A baseline model is the simplest possible prediction, here the mean of the training target. Every model must beat it. If a model cannot, it has learned nothing useful.

Question two. What does the unit of the MAE tell you? Say it to yourself first.

What I hope you said: The mean absolute error (MAE) is in the unit of the target variable, so an MAE of 2 kWh/t means the prediction error is about 2 kWh/t on average.

Question three. Why do we split the rows by equipment group? Write a word or two down.

The short answer: So that the validation set holds whole crusher groups the model has never met, which is the situation in real use.

Keep these three in mind, because today builds on them.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Class 1

rows.text: What is a baseline model for?
A baseline model is the simplest possible prediction, here the mean of the training target. Every model must beat it. If a model cannot, it has learned nothing useful.
What does the unit of the MAE tell you?
The mean absolute error (MAE) is in the unit of the target variable, so an MAE of 2 kWh/t means the prediction error is about 2 kWh/t on average.
Why do we split the rows by equipment group?
So that the validation set holds whole crusher groups the model has never met, which is the situation in real use.

objects.text: Check your own answer against these before we start today.

slides.notes:
Here are the short answers to the three questions, so you can check yourself and keep them for revision. A baseline model is the simplest possible prediction, and every model must beat it. The unit of the MAE is the unit of the target variable, so it tells you the typical size of the prediction error in plain words.

And we split by equipment group so that the validation set holds whole crusher groups the model has never seen. Did your own answer include the reason in each case?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Two possible answers: the positive class (yes, such as "overheating") and the negative class (no). The label is 1 or 0.
The probability at or above which the model predicts positive (yes).
A table of actual against predicted classes: TP, FN, FP and TN (true or false, positive or negative).
Precision: of the predicted positives, the share that are right. Recall (sensitivity): of the actual positives, the share found.
The ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate. AUC, the area under it, is 0 to 1: how well positives rank above negatives.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. Binary classification means a model with two possible answers. The positive class is the answer we look for, and the negative class is the other one. The decision threshold is the probability at or above which the model predicts positive. A confusion matrix is a table that counts our right and wrong answers.

Precision and recall are two questions about the positive answers. And the ROC curve and its AUC show how well the model ranks positives above negatives. We use each of them before the break.

title.text:
Binary classification gives a yes or no answer
that tells a control room whether to act

objects.alt: Binary classification gives a yes or no answer that tells a control room whether to act

objects.text: Binary classification has two classes: yes (positive) and no (negative). The question: is it high energy demand?

runs.text: In Class 1 (regression) the model gave a number, such as the crusher energy demand in kWh/t, scored by MAE.
Today it gives one of two classes, and we count its right and wrong answers.

slides.notes:
Last week the model gave you a number, for example the crusher energy demand in kWh/t, and we scored it by the size of the prediction error. In practice someone has to decide whether to act. So today the question is a yes or no question, which is called binary classification: is it high energy demand?

Yes is the positive class and no is the negative class. A reading arrives, the model says yes or no, and a person acts. For the crusher data the example is: yes: warn the control room. That is an illustration, and your own plant may do something different.

The data and the split are the same as Class 1. Only the question changes, so the way we score the model changes too.

title.text:
A limit on the crusher energy demand turns
each row into a positive or negative label

objects.alt: A limit on the crusher energy demand turns each row into a positive or negative label

objects.text: The label (target variable) is positive (1, yes) when the crusher energy demand is 13.5 kWh/t or more, and negative (0, no) below.

runs.text: Each dot is one row of the training set. Gold dots are positive: 24 of 58.
Validation set: 3 of 15 rows are positive.
The features are still load_pct and ambient_c.

slides.notes:
Here are the training rows again, with load on the bottom and the crusher energy demand up the side. The dashed line is the limit, 13.5 kWh/t. A row at or above the line gets the label positive, which is yes, and a row below it gets the label negative, which is no.

That rule makes the label. In the training set 24 of 58 rows are positive, and in the validation set 3 of 15 are positive. The model still sees only load and ambient temperature as features. The label is the answer it must learn to give. Which dots would you worry about most?

title.text:
The majority-class baseline always answers no, is right
on 80 percent of rows and finds no actual positive

objects.alt: The majority-class baseline always answers no, is right on 80 percent of rows and finds no actual positive

objects.text: The majority-class baseline always predicts the more common class, here no. Accuracy is the share of rows answered correctly.

runs.text: Always no is right on 12 of 15 validation rows: accuracy 0.80.
It finds none of the 3 actual positive rows.
A model must beat accuracy 0.80 and also find positive rows.

slides.notes:
Look at the validation set. 12 of the 15 rows are no, and 3 are yes. A model that says no every time is right on 12 of 15 rows, an accuracy of 0.80. That sounds good, yet it finds none of the 3 actual positive cases, and those are the ones we care about.

This is called the majority-class baseline, because it always predicts the most common class. It is the simplest model, and every real model must beat it. The validation set is imbalanced: only 3 of its 15 rows are positive. So accuracy cannot be the only measure we use today.

title.text:
The standard deviation measures how far the
values of a column typically sit from their mean

objects.alt: The standard deviation measures how far the values of a column typically sit from their mean

objects.text: Standard deviation (SD): the typical distance of a value from its mean. StandardScaler rewrites each feature as z-scores.

runs.text: load_pct: mean 59.89 %, SD 22.73 %. 33 of 58 rows lie in the gold band.
A z-score counts SDs above (+) or below (-) the mean. Red dot: training row 1.

slides.notes:
Before the classifier, one idea from statistics: the standard deviation. Each dot is one training value of load. The red line is the mean, 59.89 percent. The standard deviation, here 22.73, is the typical distance of a value from that mean, and the gold band covers one standard deviation each side.

Ambient temperature has a much smaller spread, 4.55 degrees. So the two features live on different scales. Standardisation, done by StandardScaler, rewrites each value as a z-score: how many standard deviations it sits from the mean. The bottom axis shows the same values counted that way. Why must the mean and the spread come from the training set only?

title.text:
The standard deviation and the z-score as
formulas, with training row 1 worked by hand

objects.alt: The standard deviation and the z-score as formulas, with training row 1 worked by hand

rows.text: A raw value of row i, and the number of training rows
The training mean of that column
The training standard deviation of that column
The z-score: 0 is the mean, 1 is one SD above

objects.text: StandardScaler divides by n. pandas .std() divides by n - 1 and gives 22.93 for load_pct.

slides.notes:
Here are both ideas in the usual notation. The standard deviation sigma: take each value minus the mean, square it, average the squares over the n training rows, and take the square root. For load that gives 22.73. Then the z-score: a raw value x, minus the mean mu, divided by sigma.

Training row 1 gives -0.03 for load and 1.18 for ambient temperature. One warning for your calculator checks. StandardScaler divides by n. The pandas method .std() that you used in Weeks 1 to 7 divides by n minus 1, so it gives 22.93. Both are correct; they are two versions. Check the load line by hand before we go on.

title.text:
Logistic regression passes a linear score through the
sigmoid (logistic) function, which stays between 0 and 1

objects.alt: Logistic regression passes a linear score through the sigmoid (logistic) function, which stays between 0 and 1

objects.text: The sigmoid (logistic) function turns any score s into a probability from 0 to 1.

runs.text: A probability of 0.5 means the two classes are equally likely.
The decision threshold is the probability at or above which the model predicts positive (yes), and below which it predicts negative (no).

slides.notes:
Why not use a linear function to predict yes or no?

Because a linear function keeps going, below zero and above one, and a probability cannot. Logistic regression first builds a score, which we call s, from the features, in the same way as the linear regression in Class 1. Then it passes the score through an S-shaped curve called the sigmoid, or logistic function.

Very low scores become a probability near 0, very high scores near 1, and a score of 0 becomes exactly 0.5. The gold dot is one real row with a score close to 0, so its probability sits just above 0.5. We work it out by hand in a moment.

title.text:
Logistic regression in three lines:
score, probability, prediction

objects.alt: Logistic regression in three lines: score, probability, prediction

rows.text: Intercept (bias); weights (coefficients): rise in s per standard deviation
Probability of the positive class. e = 2.718
Decision threshold: predict positive if p is at least t
The predicted class: positive (1) or negative (0)

slides.notes:
This is the whole of logistic regression in three lines. First the score s: an intercept b zero, plus a weight times each standardised feature. Our learned numbers are an intercept of -0.95, a weight of 2.64 for load and a weight of 0.49 for ambient temperature. Second, the sigmoid function turns the score into a probability p between 0 and 1.

Third, the prediction y hat: the class is positive when p is at or above the decision threshold t, and negative otherwise. We write s for the score, because the letter z already means a z-score. Both weights are positive, so more load or more heat pushes the score toward yes.

title.text:
Worked example: validation row 3 gets
p = 0.53, so the model predicts yes

objects.alt: Worked example: validation row 3 gets p = 0.53, so the model predicts yes

objects.text: Validation row 3 (record_id 17): load_pct 61.76 %, ambient_c 34.28 deg C. Actual class: positive.

runs.text: p = 0.53 is at or above 0.5: a true positive (TP).
One SD of load_pct (22.73 %) adds 2.64 to s: 0.12 per percent.
One SD of ambient_c (4.55 deg C) adds 0.49: 0.11 per deg C.

slides.notes:
This is validation row 3, which is record_id 17 in the file. After standardisation, its load is 0.08 and its ambient temperature 1.75. Multiply each by its weight, add the intercept of -0.95, and the score is 0.12. The sigmoid turns that into a probability of 0.53. At the usual decision threshold of 0.5 the model predicts yes, and the actual class was positive, so this row is a true positive (TP).

Each weight belongs to one standard deviation. One standard deviation of load is 22.73 percent, so one percentage point adds about 0.12 to the score. The products may differ in the last digit because of rounding.

title.text:
Log loss (binary cross-entropy) measures
how wrong one predicted probability is

objects.alt: Log loss (binary cross-entropy) measures how wrong one predicted probability is

objects.text: Log loss compares the probability p with the actual class y (1 or 0). It is 0 for a certain, right answer and grows fast as p moves away.

runs.text: -(y ln p + (1 - y) ln(1 - p))
Row 3, actual positive: -ln 0.53 = 0.63.
Row 11, actual negative: -ln(1 - 0.60) = 0.92.

slides.notes:
How does logistic regression learn its weights?

The same way as in Class 1: it measures its error with a loss function and walks downhill. In Class 1 the loss was the MSE. For a probability we use log loss, also called binary cross-entropy. If the row is actually positive, the loss is minus the natural log of p.

If it is actually negative, it is minus the log of one minus p. Validation row 3 is positive with p 0.53, so its loss is 0.63. Validation row 11 is negative with p 0.60, so its loss is 0.92. A confident wrong answer costs a lot: the curve shoots up.

What would the loss be for p equal to 1 on a positive row?

title.text:
The training loss is the mean log loss, and
gradient descent walks the weights downhill

objects.alt: The training loss is the mean log loss, and gradient descent walks the weights downhill

rows.text: Mean log loss over the n training rows
Error of row i: probability minus actual class
Start: all weights 0, so every p_i = 0.5
Feature j of row i (z-score); x_i0 = 1 for b0

objects.text: eta is the learning rate (step size), 0.5 here. Start by hand: slope_0 = 0.5 - 24/58 = 0.09.

slides.notes:
The training loss is the mean of the log loss over all the training rows, just as the MSE was a mean in Class 1. Gradient descent then works exactly as you saw last week: find the slope of the loss for each weight, and step a little downhill.

For log loss the slope has a friendly form. For weight j it is the mean of the error p minus y, times feature j. At the start every weight is 0, so every p is 0.5. For the intercept the slope is 0.5 minus 24 over 58, which is 0.09.

It is positive, so b zero moves down. Which way does b one move?

title.text:
scikit-learn minimises the same log loss with a faster
solver and a small L2 penalty that keeps the weights small

objects.alt: scikit-learn minimises the same log loss with a faster solver and a small L2 penalty that keeps the weights small

objects.text: LogisticRegression() minimises C x (total log loss) + 0.5 x (b1² + b2²). This L2 penalty keeps the weights small. C = 1.0.

runs.text: Gradient descent with the same penalty reaches the same weights: 2.64 and 0.49.
The lbfgs solver gets there in a few smarter steps.
The penalty works in raw units, so standardise first.

slides.notes:
Here is what scikit-learn really does. It minimises the same log loss, plus a penalty: half the sum of the squared weights, called an L2 penalty or regularisation. The intercept is not penalised. The penalty keeps the weights small, and C sets the balance: a smaller C means a stronger penalty.

Class 4 comes back to this idea with ridge regression. The curve is our own gradient descent on this loss: the training loss falls from 0.69 and the weights reach 2.64 and 0.49, the same numbers scikit-learn prints. Its solver, lbfgs, is faster. Because the penalty adds squared weights, the units of the features matter. That is one more reason to standardise.

title.text:
A decision tree classifier can also answer yes
or no, and it does not need standardisation

objects.alt: A decision tree classifier can also answer yes or no, and it does not need standardisation

objects.text: A row follows the answers down the tree to one leaf node, a yellow box. Each question is an internal node.

runs.text: A leaf predicts the majority class of its rows. (n): training rows.
max_depth = 3: at most 3 questions.
1 leaf node rests on one row: a sign of overfitting.

slides.notes:
The second model is a decision tree classifier, the same idea as Class 1 with one change at the bottom. In Class 1 each leaf node predicted an average. Now each leaf node gives the majority class of the training rows that ended there. max_depth is 3, so a row meets at most three questions.

The questions use real load and temperature, so no standardisation is needed. Look at the numbers in brackets: they count the training rows that ended in each leaf node. 1 of the leaves holds only one training row, so that rule rests on a single example. Do not read such a rule as physics.

The tree has fitted one row, which is a first sign of overfitting, and Class 3 tests it. On the validation set this tree reaches an accuracy of 0.93.

title.text:
The confusion matrix counts true
and false positives and negatives

objects.alt: The confusion matrix counts true and false positives and negatives

objects.text: Logistic regression, decision threshold 0.5, validation set. Positive class: high energy demand.

runs.text: Each of the 15 rows lands in exactly one box.
Rows: Actual class. Columns: Predicted class, as in scikit-learn.
FP is a false warning. FN is a missed positive.

slides.notes:
Here is the logistic regression on the 15 validation rows at decision threshold 0.5. Each row falls into one of four boxes. True positives, TP, are 3: the model said yes and it was yes. False negatives, FN, are 0: the model said no, but it was yes.

False positives, FP, are 1: the model said yes, but it was no. And true negatives, TN, are 11: the model said no and it was no. The four counts add to 15. Rows are the Actual class and columns are the Predicted class, the same layout scikit-learn prints. Everything else today is arithmetic on these four numbers.

title.text:
Accuracy and precision are worked out
from the four counts TP, FP, FN and TN

objects.alt: Accuracy and precision are worked out from the four counts TP, FP, FN and TN

rows.text: True positive: predicted positive, actually positive
False positive: predicted positive, actually negative
False negative: predicted negative, actually positive
True negative: predicted negative, actually negative
All rows scored: TP + TN + FP + FN

objects.text: Counts are for logistic regression at decision threshold 0.5. The majority-class baseline has accuracy 0.80.

slides.notes:
Now the formulas, with the standard names. TP, FP, FN and TN are the four counts of the confusion matrix. Accuracy asks: out of all rows, how often is the prediction right?

It is TP plus TN over all n rows: 3 plus 11, over 15, is 0.93. Precision asks: of the rows the model predicted positive, how many are really positive?

It is TP over TP plus FP, which is 3 over 4, or 0.75. Compare the accuracy with the majority-class baseline of 0.80. Which of the four counts does precision ignore?

title.text:
Recall (sensitivity) and F1: how many actual
positives we find, and one blended score

objects.alt: Recall (sensitivity) and F1: how many actual positives we find, and one blended score

rows.text: Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate): share of actual positives found
Precision: the share of the model's positive predictions that are right
The F1 score, a blend of P and R. It is low when either one is low
True positives and false negatives (previous slide)

objects.text: Same F1 from the counts: 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN) = 6 / (6 + 1 + 0) = 0.86.

slides.notes:
Recall asks: of all the rows that are actually positive, how many did we find?

That is TP over TP plus FN, which is 3 over 3, or 1.00. Recall is also called sensitivity. F1 blends precision P and recall R into one number, two P R over P plus R. With P of 0.75 and R of 1.00 we get 0.86. The note shows a second way to write it straight from the counts, and it gives the same 0.86.

F1 is low if either precision or recall is low, so you cannot hide a weak one. Please check one of these divisions on paper with me now.

title.text:
A false negative and a false positive
cost different things for a crusher

objects.text: False negative (FN)

runs.text: Predicted no, but actually yes.
Energy per tonne runs high unseen.
Energy is wasted.
Every FN lowers recall.

objects.text: False positive (FP)

runs.text: Predicted yes, but actually no.
The control room plans for demand that never comes.
It costs some time.
Every FP lowers precision.

objects.text: A false negative costs more here, so we watch recall.

slides.notes:
The two mistakes are not equal. A false negative means the model said no, and the crusher energy demand did reach its limit. Energy per tonne runs high unseen. Energy is wasted. A false positive means the model said yes and nothing happened. The control room plans for demand that never comes.

It costs some time. These descriptions are my illustration, and your own site may weigh them differently. You decide which mistake hurts more before you choose a decision threshold. In a moment we put invented prices on them, 5 for a false negative and 1 for a false positive.

Which would you protect in your own field?

title.text:
Both models give the same counts on
the same 15 rows: TP 3, FN 0, FP 1

objects.text: On these 15 rows the two models reach the same F1, so we cannot name a winner. Precision of 0.00 for the majority-class baseline means 0 of 0: it never predicts positive.

slides.notes:
Here are the two models side by side on the same 15 validation rows, with the majority-class baseline for comparison. Logistic regression has 3 true positives and 0 false negatives, with 1 false positive. The tree has 3 true positives and 0 false negatives, with 1 false positive.

The baseline has an accuracy of 0.80 but finds nothing, so its precision and recall are zero. On these 15 rows the two models reach the same F1, so we cannot name a winner. Remember that one row changes these numbers a lot when there are only 15 rows.

title.text:
Lowering the decision threshold never
lowers recall, and it can add false positives

objects.alt: Lowering the decision threshold never lowers recall, and it can add false positives

objects.text: A lower threshold predicts positive more often: recall rises or stays, and false positives can rise.

runs.text: 0.5 to 0.3: recall stays at 1.00; FP goes from 1 to 2.
0.5 to 0.7: recall goes from 1.00 to 0.67; FP goes from 1 to 0.

slides.notes:
Each dot is one validation row, placed by its probability. Gold dots are actual positives. A row at or above a dashed threshold line is predicted positive. Validation row 3 is an actual positive. Its probability is 0.53, so the model predicts positive at decision thresholds 0.3 and 0.5, and negative at 0.7.

Lowering the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3: recall stays at 1.00, and false positives (FP) go from 1 to 2. Raising it from 0.5 to 0.7: recall goes from 1.00 to 0.67, and false positives (FP) go from 1 to 0. Sliding the line left never loses a positive, and sliding it right never adds a false positive. That is the precision-recall trade-off.

title.text:
The cost of the mistakes puts a price on each one: here
a false negative costs 5 and a false positive costs 1

objects.alt: The cost of the mistakes puts a price on each one: here a false negative costs 5 and a false positive costs 1

rows.text: The cost of one false negative (a missed positive)
The cost of one false positive (a false alarm)
False negatives and false positives at the chosen threshold
The total price of the mistakes on the validation set. Lower is better

objects.text: Invented teaching costs: one missed positive costs as much as five false alarms.

slides.notes:
Now we put a price on each mistake. The cost is MISSED_COST times the false negatives, plus FALSE_ALARM_COST times the false positives. I have invented the prices for teaching: a missed high energy demand costs 5 and a false alarm costs 1. A real site would agree its own numbers with the people who pay for the mistakes.

At threshold 0.5 we have 0 false negatives and 1 false positive, so the cost is 5 times 0 plus 1 times 1, which is 1. The project uses exactly this formula with these two costs. What would the cost be at 0.3?

title.text:
The cost table picks decision threshold
0.5, the lowest cost on the validation set

objects.text: Rule: choose the threshold with the lowest cost. If two tie, take the higher threshold.

slides.notes:
This is the cost table: for each decision threshold the four counts, recall, precision and the cost. The costs are 2 at 0.3, 1 at 0.5, 5 at 0.7. The rule is simple: choose the threshold with the lowest cost, and if two tie, take the higher one, because it raises fewer alarms.

Here that is 0.5. We choose on the validation set, never on the test set. Check one cost with me by hand: five times the false negatives, plus the false positives.

title.text:
On a larger set, a lower decision threshold finds
more positives and also gives more false positives

objects.text: Illustrative example (hypothetical data), not from our data. TPR is the same as recall. Each row of this table becomes one point on a ROC curve.

slides.notes:
This table uses illustrative numbers, made up to show the trade-off clearly on a larger set. Imagine 10 actual positive rows and 90 actual negative rows. At a low decision threshold of 0.2 the model finds all 10, but it also gives 27 false positives. At a high threshold of 0.8 it gives only 1 false positive, but it finds just 4 of the 10.

The two right-hand columns are the true positive rate, the share of actual positives found, which is recall, and the false positive rate, the share of actual negatives wrongly flagged positive. Each row becomes one point on the ROC curve in a moment. Which row has the lowest cost with our prices of 5 and 1?

title.text:
Two rates give the points of the ROC curve: the false
positive rate (FPR) and the true positive rate (TPR)

objects.alt: Two rates give the points of the ROC curve: the false positive rate (FPR) and the true positive rate (TPR)

rows.text: False positive rate: share of actual negatives (FP + TN) predicted positive
True positive rate: share of actual positives (TP + FN) found. Same as recall

slides.notes:
The ROC curve needs two rates. The false positive rate, FPR, is FP over FP plus TN: of all the rows that are actually negative, what share did we wrongly flag as positive. At decision threshold 0.5 that is 1 over 12, or 0.08. The true positive rate, TPR, is the same thing as recall, also called sensitivity: 3 over 3, or 1.00.

Each threshold gives one pair of rates, and each pair is one point on the ROC graph that follows. Why is a low FPR good, and a high TPR good?

title.text:
The ROC curve plots one point for every
decision threshold: FPR across, TPR up

objects.alt: The ROC curve plots one point for every decision threshold: FPR across, TPR up

objects.text: ROC is short for receiver operating characteristic. It is a graph with one point per decision threshold.

runs.text: 16 black points, so the line is a staircase.
Your lab plot shows only the 6 corners.
Red: thresholds 0.3, 0.5, 0.7.

slides.notes:
The ROC curve is a graph, and ROC stands for receiver operating characteristic. For every decision threshold we work out two rates and plot one point: the false positive rate across, and the true positive rate up. The black dots are every threshold that changes a prediction on our rows, 16 in all, so the line climbs in steps like a staircase.

In the lab, roc_curve drops the points in the middle of a straight run, so you will see 6. The line is the same. A curve that hugs the top left corner is good, because it finds many positives with few false positives. The dashed line is random guessing. The area under the line is the AUC, here 0.97.

title.text:
AUC is the area under the ROC curve, and
on a large dataset the curve is smooth

objects.alt: AUC is the area under the ROC curve, and on a large dataset the curve is smooth

objects.text: AUC (area under the curve) is the chance that an actual positive row scores higher than an actual negative row (ties count half).

runs.text: Ours: 36 pairs (3 x 12), and 35 of 36 pairs are in the right order: AUC 0.97.
The curve is illustrative. With thousands of rows it looks smooth. AUC 0.5 is random guessing.

slides.notes:
Here is what the AUC means in words. Take one actual positive row and one actual negative row. AUC is the chance that the model gives the positive row the higher probability, and a tie counts as half. We have 3 positive rows and 12 negative rows, so 36 pairs, and 35 of them are in the right order.

That gives 0.97. The curve in the picture is illustrative. On a large dataset there are thousands of thresholds, the dots sit almost on top of each other, and the staircase becomes a smooth curve. An AUC of 0.5 is a coin flip, and 1.0 is perfect. Why is this score independent of any single decision threshold?

title.text:
With 15 rows and 3 actual
positives, every score here is shaky

objects.text: The validation set has 15 rows and only 3 actual positive rows.
If one actual positive row changed its prediction, recall would move by 0.33. One changed row moves accuracy by 0.07.
These numbers teach you how the scores work. They are too few to prove which model is better.
Class 3 shows how to test a model with more care.

slides.notes:
I want to be careful about the limits. The validation set has only 15 rows and 3 of them are actual positives. If the model got one more positive row right, the recall would move by 0.33. If it got one more row of any kind right, the accuracy would move by 0.07.

So the numbers on these slides are good for learning the scores, and weak as proof that one model beats another. The same holds for the cost table. Next class we look at tests that use more rows and give us more reason to trust a number. Keep that caution in mind in the lab.

title.text:
Summary: judge a binary classifier by
counting each kind of mistake and pricing it

objects.text: Make a label with a limit. Standardise the features into z-scores.
Logistic regression turns a score s into a probability with the sigmoid function.
It learns by gradient descent on the mean log loss, plus an L2 penalty in scikit-learn.
Count TP, FP, FN and TN, and work out accuracy, precision, recall and F1.
Choose the decision threshold with the lowest cost. AUC shows how well positives rank above negatives.

slides.notes:
Here is the whole class in five lines. Make a label from the target with a limit, and standardise the features with the training mean and standard deviation. Logistic regression turns a score into a probability with the sigmoid. It learns by walking downhill on the log loss, and scikit-learn adds a small penalty on the weights.

Count the answers in a confusion matrix, and work out accuracy, precision, recall and F1. Then price the mistakes, and choose the threshold with the lowest cost. If you can say these five lines in your own words, you are ready for the lab.

Read the workflow before you write it: impute,
standardise, fit, predict probabilities, count

"median"
X_train = imputer.fit_transform(
training_data[feature_columns])
X_valid = imputer.transform(
validation_data[feature_columns])
logistic_model = make_pipeline(
StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())
logistic_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_proba = logistic_model.predict_proba(X_valid)[:, 1]
threshold = 0.5

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: The imputer fills each missing value (NaN) with the training median (imputation).
The pipeline chains StandardScaler and LogisticRegression.
predict_proba gives a probability per class. Column 1 is the positive class.
y_proba >= threshold gives True or False. astype(int) makes it 1 or 0: y_pred.
confusion_matrix puts Actual down the side and Predicted across the top, negative first: TN and FP in the top row, FN and TP below.

slides.notes:
Before we leave the concepts, look at the workflow, with the same names as the notebook. The imputer, SimpleImputer, fills missing values with the training median. X_train is the table of training features, and y_train is the column of labels. Chain StandardScaler and the logistic regression in one pipeline called logistic_model.

Fitting it learns the means, the standard deviations and the weights from the training set only. Then ask for probabilities, and keep the column for the positive class. Compare each probability with the threshold to get y_pred, the predicted class, and count the answers in a confusion matrix.

If you can read these lines aloud in plain words, you are ready.

title.text:
Four messages you will meet,
what they mean and what to do

rows.text: A missing value (NaN) reached StandardScaler or the model
Run the imputation step (SimpleImputer with the training median)
Classification metrics can't handle a mix of binary and continuous targets
You gave probabilities where a predicted class (0 or 1) was needed
Compare y_proba with the threshold first, to get y_pred
The solver stopped before it reached the bottom of the loss. The cell still runs
Standardise the features, or raise max_iter
A cell above has not been run yet
Run all cells from the top, in order

slides.notes:
Messages are normal, and reading them is a skill. Here are the four you will most likely meet today. A NaN error means a missing value reached the model, so run the imputation step. The long message about binary and continuous targets means you gave the metric a probability where it needed a predicted class, so compare the probability with the threshold first.

A convergence warning is only a warning. It can appear when the features are on very different scales, because the solver then needs more steps. And a name error means you skipped a cell above. Read the last line of any message first.
